title: Responsibility when AI gets it wrong

sources.claim: Moffatt v. Air Canada (British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal, February 2024): the airline was held responsible for wrong refund information its website chatbot gave; the tribunal rejected the argument that the chatbot was responsible for its own statements. A small-claims decision, not binding precedent.

Mata v. Avianca (S.D.N.Y., June 22, 2023): lawyers who filed a brief citing court decisions that did not exist, generated with a chatbot and not verified, were sanctioned ($5,000); courts expect lawyers to verify every authority they cite.

jurisdiction: Canada (British Columbia); US (federal court, New York)

sections.skill: Identify the facts needed before deciding responsibility for an AI error

questions.prompt: What does responsibility for an AI error depend on?

choices.text: Only on which company made the AI tool, since tool makers are always responsible for everything

questions.intro: When AI gets something wrong, deciding who is RESPONSIBLE depends on FACTS: who made the claim to whom, what the user was told, who chose to rely on it, what checks were expected, and what contracts and laws apply. sections.skill: Gather five facts before assigning responsibility

questions.prompt: "A company's chatbot told a customer" answers which fact?

choices.text: Who made the claim, and to whom

questions.correct_answer: Who made the claim, and to whom
questions.intro: Before deciding who is responsible for an AI error, gather five facts. (1) WHO made the claim, and to whom? (2) WHAT was the user told about reliability? (3) WHO decided to rely on it? (4) WHAT checks were expected of each person? (5) WHICH contracts and laws apply? Example: a company's chatbot tells a customer a wrong price; the site never warned answers might be wrong; the customer bought based on it. Facts 1-3 point toward the company, but 4 and 5 still need checking.

questions.prompt: What does Mata mainly show?

That chatbots are always responsible for any document they help write for a court

questions.correct_answer: Professionals are expected to verify what they file
questions.intro: These examples are specific. Mata shows that professionals are expected to verify what they file; Moffatt was a small-claims decision in one Canadian province, not binding precedent elsewhere. Responsibility can be shared, and the answer may differ by place, contract and situation. Before deciding who is responsible, gather the facts first; quick blame, of the tool, the user or the company, often skips what matters.
